standard.title: Vocabulary choices for style, mood and tone
standard.description: analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to style, mood and tone
standard.prior_knowledge: Students investigate how vocabulary builds specialist knowledge, including terms with everyday and technical meanings (AC9E7LA08). They have not yet analysed how vocabulary choices create a text's distinctive style, mood and tone as interconnected qualities.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to style, mood and tone in texts.

nodes.label: Vocabulary and tone
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify vocabulary choices that create a specific tone and explain how the connotations of those choices produce that tone.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify vocabulary choices in a text that create a recognisable tone (e.g. sarcastic, reverent, anxious) and explain how the connotations of specific words produce that tone.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how a range of vocabulary choices across a text consistently build a tone, explaining how individual word connotations accumulate into a tonal effect.
wider: Compare how the same subject is treated with different tonal registers in two texts (e.g. a news report vs a satirical piece), and explain what vocabulary shifts produce the tonal difference
Examine how a sarcastic tone is constructed through the gap between vocabulary connotation and implied meaning

response_modes.reason: Tone is easy to perceive but hard to analyse — students often say 'the tone is sarcastic' without being able to connect it to specific vocabulary features. Multiple text types with contrasting tones help students build the analytical vocabulary for naming how tone is made.

success_criteria: Student identifies specific vocabulary choices and names a tone they contribute to
Student explains how the connotations of those words produce the named tonal quality

nodes.label: Vocabulary and mood
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how vocabulary choices create and sustain mood — the emotional atmosphere of a text — and distinguish mood from tone.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify vocabulary choices that create a recognisable mood in a text and explain how they create that atmosphere for the reader.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how vocabulary choices across a passage create and sustain mood, distinguishing mood (the atmosphere created for the reader) from tone (the author's attitude).
wider: Analyse how mood shifts are created through vocabulary change within a text, and examine what effect these shifts have on reader response
Compare how mood is created through vocabulary in a written text versus a moving image — examining whether visual and verbal mood-making use equivalent or different devices

response_modes.reason: Students routinely conflate mood with tone or with character emotion. Seeing mood created across different text types — narrative, poetry, film — where neither the author's attitude nor a character's feeling is the primary effect helps students secure the distinct concept.

success_criteria: Student identifies vocabulary choices contributing to mood and names the mood created
Student distinguishes mood from tone in at least one example — explaining the difference between the atmosphere experienced and the author's attitude
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate mood (reader atmosphere) and tone (author attitude) produce systematically muddled style analyses at N3 — the vocabulary/style node requires the mood/tone distinction to be operative.

nodes.label: Vocabulary and style
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to an author's distinctive style — the recognisable patterns of language use that characterise their writing.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify vocabulary features that contribute to a text's style and explain how they characterise that text's distinctive voice or manner.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how vocabulary choices across a text contribute to its stylistic effectiveness — including how the vocabulary's register, precision, rhythm and connotative range define a recognisable style.
wider: Compare the vocabulary styles of two texts by the same author and identify consistent stylistic features that mark authorial identity
Examine how an author's vocabulary style serves their purpose — why a particular style is effective for this text's context and audience

response_modes.reason: Style, mood and tone are interconnected — a text's vocabulary choices produce all three simultaneously. The integration node asks students to coordinate their understanding of all three into a unified analysis of how vocabulary choices contribute to a text's overall effect.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Vocabulary analysis for style connects directly to literary appreciation (AC9E9LE04) and to students' own writing. The analysis of authorial style — what makes a writer's voice distinctive and effective — is rich pedagogical territory for Y9 and motivates both close reading and creative experimentation.
success_criteria: Student identifies vocabulary features that contribute to a recognisable style
Student explains how the vocabulary choices are effective for this text's purpose and audience
